                                      PROJECT NO. 58481


LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                          §            PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
              STANDARDS                             §                         OF TEXAS
                                                    §


Voltus appreciates the opportunity to comment on the Proposal For Publication (PFP) memo and
recognizes the Commission's effort to implement PURA §37.0561. However, the intermediate
agreement and interconnection agreement as described place undue emphasis on backup
generation resources. While not explicitly stated in the PFP memo, our understanding is that
backup generation resource capacity will have some bearing on a large load’s approval to
interconnect and time to interconnection.


Voltus proposes that sites also be given the opportunity to engage in a Bring Your Own Capacity
(BYOC) program, and that the impacts of BYOC be taken into account for large load approval to
interconnect and time to interconnection. BYOC is an arrangement in which a large load relies
on grid power under normal conditions, but initiates a response from resources such as
demand-side flexibility during periods of system stress. Interconnection studies should consider
“electrically proximate” or “adjacent” grid assets—assets that can mitigate the constraints
imposed by new loads where those constraints actually occur—netted against load
withdrawals.Though not “within the fenceline”, such “adjacent” grid assets may have the same
benefit to the grid as colocated loads, and so should have the same benefit for interconnection
approval and timing.


Texas Utilities Code (PURA) § 37.0561(e) states the following:


“The independent organization shall establish a threshold before or during an energy emergency
alert at which the organization may issue reasonable notice that large load customers with
on-site backup generating facilities may be directed to either deploy the customer ’s on-site
backup generating facilities or curtail load.” In light of this requirement, it is Voltus’s position
 that large loads should have the option to implement BYOC instead of curtailing their own load
or starting up their generation assets.


Benefits of BYOC as it relates to the PFP are as follows:


    1.​ BYOC delivers a faster solution. A Google-sponsored paper found that by “combining
        flexible grid connections with bring-your-own capacity (BYOC) arrangements, data
        centers can reach full operation years sooner while maintaining reliability and improving
        affordability for all customers.” By comparison, there is a nationwide backlog in the
        development of gas-fired power for data centers, and it could create wait times of 5-7
        years. ERCOT has long been a fast-moving, business-friendly market. It is imperative
        that the Commission reduce this delay by implementing a BYOC option, or risk falling
        behind other jurisdictions in its ability to attract new business.1​


    2.​ BYOC provides a financial hedge for uptime-sensitive large loads. Loads that cannot
        tolerate frequent shutdowns must run backup generation, which can be costly and subject
        to permitting limitations. BYOC would allow these loads to procure load reduction from
        other nearby loads at a fixed rate. ​


    3.​ BYOC will align financial responsibility for large loads that impose new costs upon the
        system by having them pay to provide a service that mitigates those impacts. BYOC will
        ensure that infrastructure costs can become a source of revenue rather to other ratepayers,
        who are concerned that today they may have to cover costs for new large loads. The
        Google study mentioned above found that BYOC, combined with flexible connections,
        would “mitigate new system buildout and shift remaining costs onto the data center”. In
        other words, BYOC would hold the large load responsible for procuring and financing
        demand-side resources, which would in turn delay infrastructure upgrades, reducing
        system costs.



1
 According to the white paper Flexible Data Centers: A Faster, More Affordable Path to Power: “A 500-MW data
center using flexible grid connection + BYOC can reach full operation in roughly two years; three to five years
faster than traditional interconnection processes”, page 5.
        4.​ BYOC can reduce total system costs. As shown in the chart below, when studied on
           PJM’s system, results showed that BYOC could yield $78 million in avoided costs.2
           Further, BYOC delays the need for infrastructure upgrades and instead puts earnings back
           in the hands of local businesses.




       5.​ Casting a wider net on eligible technologies (BYOG and BYOC) will inherently increase
           competition in the market for enabling large loads, thus bringing down costs and making
           Texas a more attractive place to build.


Voltus proposes the following changes:
       A.​ Provide a BYOC alternative to traditional backup generation. Under section F
           (Interconnection Agreement) item 6 (Backup generating facilities), the Commission
           provides instructions for disclosure of backup generation facilities. Voltus suggests that
           BYOC be added as an alternative in this section.
               a.​ Voltus also suggests that the Commission add BYOC to section C (Definitions),
                    either as its own defined term or as a subitem of Backup generating facilities.
       B.​ Expedite interconnection for large loads that implement a BYOC program. Distributed
           capacity assets are installed today across critical footprints, are readily installable en
           masse, and may be aggregated into utility-scale assets on a timeline of months rather than

2
    Flexible Data Centers: A Faster, More Affordable Path to Power, page 6.
 years. Wholesale market demand response—which is primarily commercial and
industrial load—has been contributing to affordability and reliability for over a decade
and can scale rapidly. In 2023 alone, the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”) added
approximately 431 MW new demand response resource capability, equivalent to a large
power plant. Another 500 MW power plant could be added by interconnecting to the
distribution system a mere 200 batteries of 1-5 MW size. Residential resources can also
be mobilized: a recent report by Rewiring America identifies an additional 93 GW of
needed data center capacity through 2029 but also finds that “hyperscalers could more
than meet their total planned capacity needs by paying for battery storage as well as
rooftop solar for homes well suited for it.”
